summary: This unit teaches you to obtain and manage consultancy services for a Jamaican public body. You will learn to decide whether a consultant is needed, build a business case and cost estimate, write terms of reference, select a consultant fairly under the procurement rules, score proposals, agree a contract, manage performance, variations and payments, secure knowledge transfer and evaluate the result.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It prepares you to **obtain and manage consultancy services**: to bring in outside expertise when your agency needs it, to choose the consultant fairly, and to make sure the agency gets what it paid for.

A **consultant** is an individual or firm hired for a specific job that needs skills, independence or capacity the agency does not have. A **consultancy** has a clear start, a clear end and defined **deliverables**. Typical Jamaican examples are a review of a records system, a redesign of a licensing process, a training needs study, an evaluation of a programme, a feasibility study, or the design of a computer system.

In a public body the money is public money. Every step, from deciding that a consultant is needed to paying the final invoice, must be **fair, open and good value**, and must leave a record that an auditor can follow.
**Who it is for:** managers and officers in ministries, agencies, statutory bodies and municipal corporations who commission, evaluate or oversee consultancy work.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Decide whether a consultant is needed
Define the problem, compare using a consultant with using your own staff, and confirm the money is approved.
Work out fees, expenses, contingency and GCT at the current rate, and check the sums twice.
State the background, objectives, scope, deliverables, timing and what the agency will supply.
Follow the procurement rules: shortlist, issue a request for proposals, score technical quality first, then price.
Declare interests, keep bidders at arm's length and treat everyone equally.
Choose the contract type and include the clauses that protect the agency.
Run the inception, monitor progress, control variations, accept deliverables and pay against them.
Transfer knowledge, keep the file, evaluate the consultancy and report.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper**, including short sums on fees, scores and payments.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms and calculations) and longer answers.
**Group practical tasks**: writing the terms of reference and evaluation plan for a consultancy, and managing a failing consultancy through a progress review meeting and recovery plan.

blocks.note: Learn the abbreviations and sums: TOR, EOI, RFP, QCBS, the financial score formula, and payments as a percentage of the contract price.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Is a consultant the right answer?

blocks.h: Start with the problem, not the solution

blocks.p: When a senior officer says 'bring in consultants to fix the unit', do not start looking for consultants. First **define the problem and the result the agency needs**: What exactly is wrong? How do we know? What would 'fixed' look like? Who is affected? A vague problem leads to a vague contract and a report nobody uses.

head: Consider
A consultant suits when ...
Your own staff suit when ...
rows: The agency needs a specialist skill it lacks
The skill exists in the agency
The need is short and set
An outside, unbiased view is needed (an evaluation, a review of a sensitive matter)
Inside knowledge matters more than independence
Staff are fully committed elsewhere for a limited period
Staff have time, or can be released
Fees are justified by the benefit and cost less than recruiting
A post or service contract is cheaper over time
The agency wants to learn from an expert
The agency wants to build its own long-term capacity

blocks.p: A consultancy is **not** the right route for **ongoing core work**. If a municipal corporation plans to pay a consultant to process its payroll every month for years, it needs a post or a service contract, not a consultancy. A consultant is also not a way to avoid a recruitment freeze or to hide a decision.

blocks.h: The business case and approved funds

blocks.p: A short **business case** states the problem, why a consultant is needed, the expected benefits, the options considered, the estimated cost and the source of funds. Confirm that **money is approved in the budget** before going to the market. Otherwise the agency may commit public money it cannot pay and break the public financial rules.

The fee for a consultant is **days × daily rate**. Add expenses (travel, printing, workshops) and a **contingency**. Show GCT separately: add **GCT at the current rate** if the consultant charges it, and ask your finance officer to confirm how it is treated. The sums below exclude GCT.

blocks.note: Do the sums twice, and write the working beside each line. A fee estimate is checked against what the proposals later say, so a clear estimate also helps you judge whether a price is reasonable.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **A quick sum:** 25 days at J$40,000 a day is 25 × 40,000 = J$1,000,000 before GCT.

The **terms of reference (TOR)** is the document that sets out the **background, scope, outputs and timing** of the consultancy. It is the most important document you will write: bidders price from it, the contract rests on it and you will judge the consultant's work against it.

head: Heading
What it says
Why it matters
rows: The agency, its services, the problem and what has been done so far
What is in, and what is out; the places, units and period covered
The specific outputs: reports, manuals, systems, training, with standards and formats
You can check and accept them
Start and end dates, reporting dates and milestones
Allows planning and payment against milestones
The staff, data, space and decisions the agency will supply, and by when
Bidders can price and plan accurately
Who the consultant reports to, meetings, progress reports
How payment is linked to deliverables; confidentiality; ownership of outputs

blocks.p: An **activity** is something the consultant does: 'hold workshops with staff'. A **deliverable** is something that is handed over: 'a final report with costed recommendations', 'a training manual', 'a working database'. Payment should be tied to deliverables.

blocks.h: A weak TOR and a strong TOR

head: Weak
Strong
rows: 'Review and improve customer service.' (No outputs, no standard, no deadline.)

'Review customer service at the three parish offices over 12 weeks and deliver: (1) a work plan within 10 days; (2) a report of findings with data from at least 300 customers; (3) a costed improvement plan with priorities; (4) two training sessions for 40 staff. Standards: plain English, draft for comment two weeks before the final report.'

ul: State the **client inputs**: staff time, access to data, office space, a named contact. If you do not say what you will supply, bidders must guess and will add a margin to the price.
Make sure objectives are **specific and measurable**.
Have a colleague who did not write it read it. Test whether the deliverables would be enough for you to make the decision you have in mind.

blocks.note: A firm that helped to write the TOR may have shaped it to suit itself, which is an unfair advantage. Such a firm should normally not be allowed to bid for the work, or the advantage must be removed.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The **procurement rules for public bodies** aim at **fair competition, transparency and value for money**. They set the methods and the approval levels by the type and value of the work. Follow your agency's procurement procedures and the guidance of your procurement officer or committee. This unit refers to the rules by purpose and does not quote thresholds or section numbers.

head: Method
How it works
Suits
rows: Proposals are scored on technical quality and price together, using stated weights
Choose the best technical proposal, then negotiate the price
Complex work where quality is the main factor
The budget is stated; choose the best technical proposal within it
Simple, well-defined work with a fixed sum
Choose the lowest price among firms passing a minimum quality
Only where the rules allow, and the reason is recorded

blocks.p: A manager cannot hire a friend or a past consultant without competition simply because 'she is good'. Direct selection is for the cases the rules permit, with the reason **recorded**, and approved at the right level. Emergency procurement after a disaster may allow quicker methods, but the reasons, the limits and the record still apply. **Do not split** a requirement into smaller contracts to avoid a threshold or a competition.

flow: Approved need, budget and TOR
Request for expressions of interest (EOI)
Shortlist by scoring against published criteria
Request for proposals (RFP) to the shortlist
Answer questions to all, in writing
Receive proposals by the closing time
Evaluate technical proposals, then open prices
Combine scores and rank
Negotiate with the top-ranked firm
Notify bidders, award and sign the contract

blocks.p: A notice asking firms to show their interest and experience is a **request for expressions of interest (EOI)**. When twelve firms respond, draw up the shortlist by **scoring each firm against the criteria published in the notice** (for example relevant experience, similar assignments, qualified staff), not by personal preference. Usually between three and six firms are shortlisted.

The **RFP** invites the shortlisted firms to send a **technical proposal** and a **price proposal**. It includes the TOR, instructions, the **evaluation criteria and their weights**, how price will be scored, the closing date and time, and a draft contract.

ul: **Questions from bidders**: answer every question in writing and send the question and answer to **all** shortlisted firms, without naming who asked.
**Closing time**: a proposal that arrives after the published closing time is rejected and returned or recorded unopened. Treat all firms alike.
**Contact**: all contact goes through the named officer in writing.

blocks.p: Many public bodies score the **technical proposals first**, then open the price proposals, so that quality is judged without being influenced by price. A **minimum technical score** (a pass mark) is set; a proposal below it is **not considered further**, however low its price.

flow: Panel members score technical proposals independently
Panel meets and agrees technical scores, with reasons
Firms below the minimum score are removed
Price proposals of the remaining firms are opened
Calculate financial scores
Apply the weights and add the scores
Rank the firms and record everything

blocks.p: **Financial score** = lowest valid price ÷ firm's price × 100. **Combined score** = (technical score × technical weight) + (financial score × price weight).
An RFP uses weights **70% technical and 30% price** with a **75-point minimum**. Three firms respond:

head: Firm
Technical score
Price (J$)
Result
rows: Below the minimum: not considered, and its price is ignored

blocks.p: The lowest **valid** price is that of Firm Q: J$4,400,000. Q's financial score is 4,400,000 ÷ 4,400,000 × 100 = **100**. P's is 4,400,000 ÷ 5,500,000 × 100 = **80**.

Q ranks first with 86.0 against 85.6. The panel records all scores and reasons, checks the sums, confirms no member has a conflict, and then invites Q to negotiate, keeping P as the reserve. Notice that Firm R's very low price made no difference: it failed the technical minimum.

blocks.note: The lowest valid price must be found **after** removing firms that failed the minimum technical score. If you use the price of a firm that has been rejected, every financial score is wrong.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Every panel member **declares any link** with a bidding firm (family, business, friendship) and **steps off the panel** if there is one.
Panel members must **keep their scoring confidential** until the process is complete.
**Decline** any invitation, gift or hospitality from a bidder, and keep all contact through the formal channel.
Never reveal one firm's price or ideas to another.
If a panel member sees a price early by mistake, report it to the chair so that the process can be protected or repeated.
Keep a **written record** of the evaluation: it must withstand an audit or a complaint.

blocks.p: Negotiate with the top-ranked firm only on matters that do not change the basis of the competition: **work-plan detail, timing, client inputs**, and contract terms. If agreement cannot be reached, move to the next-ranked firm. Tell all bidders the result. An unsuccessful bidder who asks why it lost should be offered a **debriefing on its own proposal's strengths and weaknesses**, not on other firms' proposals.

head: Type
How the consultant is paid
Suits
Risk
rows: One agreed total, paid against deliverables, whatever days are worked
Clear, fixed outputs that can be priced in advance
Variations must be handled with care
Daily or hourly rate for the time actually worked, with a cap
Cost may grow; time must be checked and approved
An agreed fee to be available, or rates for tasks as ordered

head: Clause
Why it matters
rows: The TOR and the accepted proposal attached
The scope and deliverables are binding
They may be replaced only with an equal or better person approved in writing
The agency pays only for work that meets the agreed standard
The agency owns, or has the right to use, what the consultant produces, such as a training manual or a system
The consultant must protect any personal or sensitive data, use it only for the work, and return or destroy it at the end
Changes to scope, time or price must be agreed in writing before the work starts
Reports, penalties or the right to withhold payment and to end the contract
How and when either side may end the contract
Steps to follow, for example discussion, then mediation, then other steps in the contract
The consultant declares conflicts and works honestly

blocks.p: A lump-sum contract of **J$7,500,000** pays **15%** when the inception report is accepted, **25%** when the interim report is accepted, **40%** when the draft final report is accepted and **20%** when the final report is accepted.

After the interim report is accepted, J$1,125,000 + J$1,875,000 = **J$3,000,000** (40%) has been paid. A **large advance** is not wise: payments should follow **accepted deliverables**, so the agency pays only for work that meets the agreed standard. Check the sums twice and make sure the percentages add up to 100.

blocks.note: A contract is signed only after it has gone through the approval levels in the procurement rules. Never allow work to start on a verbal promise.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: At the **inception meeting** the contract manager and consultant confirm the TOR, the work plan, the team, the client inputs, reporting routines and risks. The consultant then writes an **inception report** to confirm the consultant's understanding, method and work plan. The client accepts or comments in writing before the main work proceeds.

If the team leader who attends is **not the person named in the proposal**, the contract manager must require an **equal or better replacement, approved in writing**, as the contract says. Key staff are part of what the agency chose.

head: Role
What the person does
rows: Contract manager (a named client officer with clear authority)
Day-to-day contact; checks progress; confirms inputs; reviews drafts; recommends payment
Gives direction, resolves problems, accepts key outputs, approves variations of importance
Checks invoices against accepted deliverables and the payment schedule
Leads the work and answers to the contract manager for quality and time

ul: Agree a **reporting routine**: for example a short fortnightly progress report and monthly meetings.
Compare progress with the work plan and milestones.
Keep an **action log** of what was agreed and by whom.
Provide the **client inputs** on time: late data or access is often the real cause of delay.
If a consultant fails to send progress reports, **raise it in writing first and agree how to fix it**.

blocks.p: If staff refuse to give data because they fear job cuts, the manager should **explain the purpose of the work** and **agree how the data will be used**: mistrust will slow the work, and the consultant cannot fix it alone.

A **variation** is a formal written change to the scope, time or price of the contract. A variation must be **agreed and approved before the extra work starts**. **Scope creep** is the gradual, uncontrolled growth of the work beyond what the contract covers, through small requests that are never recorded.

**Worked example.** A J$7,500,000 contract adds 12 days of work at J$40,000 a day. The variation costs 12 × 40,000 = J$480,000. The percentage increase is 480,000 ÷ 7,500,000 × 100 = **6.4%**. The new contract value is J$7,980,000. Check whether the variation is within your authority and the procurement rules.

flow: Consultant submits the draft
Contract manager checks it against each TOR item
Staff and the steering committee comment
Written comments go to the consultant
Consultant corrects and resubmits
Client accepts in writing
Finance pays the invoice for that milestone

blocks.p: A draft that is well written but **does not answer every question in the TOR** is not complete. Return it with written comments against the TOR **before accepting** it, and do not pay for that milestone until it is accepted.

head: Step
Action
rows: Gather evidence: dates, reports, quality gaps, absent team members
Raise the problems **in writing**, citing the contract and TOR
Hold a meeting and agree a **recovery plan** with revised dates and the key staff position
Withhold payment for work not accepted, as the contract allows
If the recovery plan fails, follow the contract's termination steps and consider the cost of continuing, replacing or ending

blocks.p: If the consultant and the agency disagree on whether a deliverable meets the TOR, **discuss it and use the dispute steps in the contract** first. Keep a record, remain courteous and escalate only as the contract allows.

ul: **Favouritism**: use competition as the rules require, and record any direct selection with its reason.
**Conflicts of interest**: panel members and the contract manager declare links.
**Splitting** a requirement to avoid competition.
**Paying for work not done**: pay only against accepted deliverables.
**Confidentiality**: protect personal and commercial information.

blocks.p: **Knowledge transfer** is the passing of the consultant's skills and know-how to the agency's own staff, so that the benefit lasts after the consultant leaves. To make sure staff can keep a new system running, build **training, manuals and staff shadowing into the contract** and make them deliverables. Name the staff who will receive the knowledge from the start.

blocks.h: Relying on the same consultant for years

blocks.p: The main risk of using the same consultant repeatedly is that the agency becomes **dependent** and **loses its own skills**, and may stop testing the market for value. Keep competing the work and keep building your own staff's skills.

flow: All deliverables accepted in writing
Final invoice checked and paid
Data, equipment and passwords returned; confidential data returned or destroyed
Intellectual property and source files handed over
Knowledge transfer completed
Consultancy evaluated
File closed and stored

blocks.p: The most useful question is: **Did the outputs meet the TOR, on time and within budget, and are they being used?** Ask the steering committee and the staff who worked with the consultant. Compare with the TOR, the time, the cost (including approved variations), the quality of the outputs and the benefits to the agency. Record the lessons for the next consultancy and for the consultant's performance record if the agency keeps one.

Keep the **complete file** of the consultancy: business case, TOR, advertisements, shortlist, evaluation scores and reasons, contract, variations, reports, payment records and the evaluation. It must be kept so that the agency can **show auditors how public money was spent**, and answer any complaint or request under the access to information law.

ul: define the problem and decide whether a consultant or my own staff should do the work.
say why a consultancy is wrong for ongoing core work.
prepare a cost estimate with fees, expenses, contingency and GCT at the current rate.
write terms of reference with objectives, scope, deliverables, timing and client inputs.
tell a deliverable from an activity and spot a weak TOR.
explain the selection methods and when direct selection is allowed.
run a call for expressions of interest, a shortlist and a request for proposals fairly.
answer bidders' questions to all, and reject late proposals.
score technical proposals first, apply the minimum score and work out financial and combined scores.
declare and manage conflicts of interest and decline gifts and lunches from bidders.
choose between a lump-sum and a time-based contract and include the protecting clauses.
work out payments as percentages of the contract price.
run an inception, monitor progress and handle key-staff changes.
control variations and scope creep, accept deliverables against the TOR and pay only for accepted work.
deal with a failing consultant, plan knowledge transfer and evaluate the consultancy.

terms: An individual or firm hired for a specific job needing skills the agency lacks.
The document setting out the background, scope, outputs and timing of a consultancy.
A specific output the consultant must hand over, such as a report or manual.
A notice asking firms to show their interest and experience, to draw up a shortlist.
The firms chosen from the responses to be invited to submit proposals.
The document inviting shortlisted firms to send technical and price proposals.
Quality- and cost-based selection: proposals scored on quality and price together.
The pass mark a proposal must reach before its price is considered.
A contract where the consultant is paid one agreed total for set outputs.
The early report where the consultant confirms the method and work plan.
The named client officer who oversees the consultant day to day.
A group that gives direction, resolves issues and accepts key outputs.
A formal written change to a contract's scope, time or price.
The gradual, uncontrolled growth of the work beyond what the contract covers.
The passing of the consultant's skills to the client's own staff.
The right to own and use what the consultant creates.
Appointing a consultant without competition, only where the rules allow.

c1.title: Market-fee review at a municipal corporation
c1.text: The Municipal Corporation of St Thomas finds that market-fee income has fallen for two years. The mayor suggests hiring a consultant. The finance director, Mrs Karen Powell, plans a four-person-month review. She estimates that a team leader will need 20 days at J$55,000 a day and an analyst 30 days at J$32,000 a day, with J$250,000 for expenses and a 10% contingency on fees and expenses, before GCT. She has not yet checked whether the money is in the approved budget.

c2.title: Scoring three proposals
c2.text: A ministry is evaluating proposals for a training-needs study. The RFP uses a 70% weight for technical quality and 30% for price, with a minimum technical score of 75 points. Firm P scored 88 and bid J$5,500,000. Firm Q scored 80 and bid J$4,400,000. Firm R scored 72 and bid J$3,300,000. The financial score is the lowest valid price divided by the firm's price, times 100.

c3.title: Contract and payment schedule
c3.text: A parish agency signs a lump-sum consultancy contract for J$7,500,000 to design a visitor-information system. Payment is 15% on acceptance of the inception report, 25% on the interim report, 40% on the draft final report and 20% on the final report. Midway, the director asks for 12 extra days of work at J$40,000 a day, to cover a second site.

c4.title: Late and incomplete consultancy
c4.text: Mr Garfield Thompson is the contract manager for a ministry consultancy to design a farm-records system, with eight deliverables listed in the TOR. The draft final report arrives three weeks late. It covers five of the eight deliverables well. The consultant's team leader, named in the proposal, has attended only one meeting, and a junior officer has done most of the work.

c5.title: Integrity at the evaluation panel
c5.text: A public agency is buying a consultancy worth about J$12,000,000. The procurement officer proposes to split it into three contracts of J$4,000,000 so that the approval will be quicker. Separately, a panel member accidentally sees the price envelope of one bidder before the technical scoring is finished. A director also suggests that, because a hurricane has just damaged offices, the agency should hire a former colleague at once without competition.

c6.title: A new system and the staff who must run it
c6.text: A consultant has built a new records database for a ministry's registry. The final report is accepted and the final payment is due. The registry has three clerks who will use the system and one IT officer. The contract did not include training or a user manual.

questions.q: What is the total estimate for the review, before GCT?
Before inviting any firm, what should Mrs Powell confirm about the budget, and why?
o: That the budget is larger than the estimate, so it can all be spent at once
That the mayor has approved it, which makes competition unnecessary
That the consultant's GCT will be paid from the contingency
That the money is approved, so no unfunded commitment is made
questions.why: Public money must not be committed before it is approved. Without confirmed funds, the corporation may not be able to pay the contract.

questions.q: Which of these is the strongest reason to use a consultant for the market-fee review?
o: The finance department would prefer not to look at its own collection figures
The mayor wants to see a report before the end of the quarter
It needs a specialist skill and an outside view for a set period
A consultant is always cheaper than the corporation's own staff
questions.why: A consultant suits a short, specific need for skills or independence that the agency lacks. Convenience, politics or an assumption about cost are not good reasons.

questions.q: Which firms are considered in the price comparison, and what is the lowest valid price?
o: P, Q and R, and J$3,300,000
P and Q only, and J$4,400,000
Q and R only, and J$3,300,000
P only, and J$5,500,000
questions.why: Firm R scored 72, below the minimum of 75, so it is out and its price is ignored. The lowest price among P and Q is J$4,400,000.

questions.q: What are the financial scores of P and Q?
o: P 100 and Q 80
P 80 and Q 100
P 80 and Q 60
P 75 and Q 100

questions.q: Which firm ranks first, and by how much?
o: Q, with 86.0 against 85.6
P, with 85.6 against 86.0
Q, with 100 against 80
P, with 88 against 80
questions.why: P: 88 × 0.7 = 61.6 plus 80 × 0.3 = 24, giving 85.6. Q: 80 × 0.7 = 56 plus 100 × 0.3 = 30, giving 86.0. Q is first by 0.4, so the weights matter.

questions.q: Firm R offers by far the lowest price. Why is it not considered further?
o: Its price is too low to be believed and must be rejected on that ground
Its price was opened before the technical scores were agreed
The panel may only consider the two highest technical scores
It failed the minimum technical score, which applies whatever the price
questions.why: The minimum technical score is a pass mark set in advance. A firm that fails it is out, whatever it bids.

questions.q: How much has been paid after the interim report is accepted?
What is the percentage increase in the contract if the 12 extra days are approved?
What must happen before the consultant starts the extra days for the second site?
o: The director tells the consultant to start, and the paperwork follows later
A written variation is agreed and approved under the contract rules
The consultant starts, and the extra cost is absorbed in the final invoice
The team leader and the director agree by telephone, and a note is kept
questions.why: Changes to scope, time or price are agreed and approved in writing before the work starts. Otherwise the agency risks scope creep and a payment dispute.

questions.q: Why is it better to link the payments to accepted deliverables than to pay a large advance?
o: The agency pays only for work that has met the agreed standard
The consultant will accept a lower price if it is paid late
It makes the contract easier to sign without an approval
It ensures the consultant has no cash-flow problems at the start
questions.why: Payments tied to accepted deliverables protect public money, because the agency pays for what it has received and checked.

questions.q: How should Mr Thompson respond to the draft that covers five of the eight deliverables?
o: Accept it, since most of the work is of good quality and the date has passed
Accept it and ask the consultant to finish the other three after the final invoice
Pay half of the milestone now and move on to the next stage of work
Return it with comments against the TOR and withhold that milestone payment
questions.why: A draft that does not meet the TOR is not ready for acceptance. Written comments against the TOR and withholding payment for that milestone protect the agency.

questions.q: The team leader named in the proposal has attended only one meeting. What is the correct step?
o: Accept the junior officer as the team leader, since the work is being done
Ask the consultant to bring the team leader only to the final meeting
Reduce the contract price, without raising it in a meeting
Require the named staff, or an equal or better one approved in writing
questions.why: Key staff are part of what the agency chose. The contract should require them or an approved equal or better replacement.

questions.q: What is the best way to deal with the lateness and the gaps in the work?
o: End the contract at once and appoint the next-ranked firm
Say nothing until the final report, to give the consultant time
Raise them in writing, meet, and agree a recovery plan with new dates
Complete the missing three items with the agency's own staff
questions.why: Problems are raised in writing and a recovery plan is agreed first. Ending the contract is a later step if the plan fails, and follows the contract's termination steps.

questions.q: Why is it wrong to split the J$12,000,000 requirement into three contracts of J$4,000,000?
o: It will make the contracts too small for any consultant to bid on
It avoids the approval and competition that the full value needs
It increases the cost of the work by repeating the evaluation
It is correct, because each contract is then below the limit
questions.why: Splitting to stay under a threshold defeats the procurement rules, which set controls by value. It is a serious integrity risk.

questions.q: The panel member sees one bidder's price early by mistake. What should she do?
o: Tell the chair at once, so the process can be protected
Say nothing, as she cannot un-see it and the scoring is nearly done
Tell the other panel members so that no one has an unfair advantage
Score that firm's technical proposal last and carry on
questions.why: The early sight could affect the fairness of the evaluation. She must report it to the chair, who decides how to protect the process.

questions.q: The director suggests hiring a former colleague without competition after the hurricane. What is the correct position?
o: Only if the rules permit it, with the reason recorded and approved
Any hiring after a disaster can be done without competition or records
It is acceptable provided that the colleague charges less than the budget
It is never allowed in a public body, even after a disaster has struck
questions.why: Emergency procurement may allow faster methods, but only as the rules allow, with the reasons and limits recorded and approved. 'She is good' is not enough.

questions.q: The consultant's work is accepted but no training was in the contract. What is the main risk, and how could it have been avoided?
o: The system will be too expensive, and the price should have been lowered
The consultant will refuse to be paid, and a penalty should have been added
The registry will have too many clerks, and the posts should have been cut
Staff cannot run it; training, manuals and shadowing belonged in the contract
questions.why: Without knowledge transfer, the agency depends on the consultant. Training, manuals and shadowing built into the contract, as deliverables, prevent this.

questions.q: The competition goes ahead as one contract. In negotiation, the top-ranked firm then demands a 30% price rise. What should the agency do?
o: Accept the new price, since the firm was ranked first
Award the work to the cheapest firm that bid, whatever its score
Record the reasons and invite the next-ranked firm to negotiate
Cancel the competition and appoint a firm of its own choice
questions.why: Negotiation covers details such as the work plan and timing, not a change of price that alters the competition. If agreement fails, the agency records the reasons and moves to the next-ranked firm.

questions.q: Before the ministry pays the final invoice, which handover step should it make sure is done?
o: The consultant's team leader signs a statement that the team enjoyed the work
Data, source files and passwords handed over, confidential data returned
The registry clerks write a letter of thanks to the consultant's firm
The consultant's laptops are entered in the ministry's asset register
questions.why: Closing a consultancy means getting what was paid for: the outputs, files and access, plus the return or destruction of any confidential data the consultant held.
